html:
The Manusmriti, or Laws of Manu, is the best known of the Sanskrit texts on dharma: duty, law and right conduct. It was composed by Brahmin authors, probably in the 2nd or 3rd century CE, and credited to Manu, the first man.

In about 2,700 verses it sets out how each kind of person should live. Society has four ranks, the varnas: Brahmins who teach and perform rites, Kshatriyas who rule and fight, Vaishyas who farm and trade, and Shudras who serve. Duties, punishments and even rates of interest differ by rank. A woman, it says, should be under her father, then her husband, then her sons. It also covers kingship, courts, debts, inheritance and penance.

It is an ideal written by one group, and how far it was followed is unclear. Real practice varied by region and caste; see the caste system.

It gained new force under British rule. William Jones translated it in 1794, and the courts used it as "Hindu law". For that reason reformers made it their target. B. R. Ambedkar burnt a copy in public in 1927 during the Mahad Satyagraha.
